[This article was first published on R on kieranhealy.org, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)

New York City month continues here at Kieran Healy Industries, an effort that will eventually produce something properly scholarly in nature. But in the meantime—and with my apologies to the many great urbanists of times past—we can enjoy ourselves by messing around with some data. Specifically, New York’s 311 Services and Complaints data. The 311 phone line and website is the the main point of contact for city services when it’s not an emergency. The city logs all the calls it gets and makes anonymized data available publicly via NYC OpenData. I got every record from 2010 to 2025 and packaged it up for R. The package is really just a front-end for a big parquet file managed by DuckDB. DuckDB offers a very powerful in-memory database engine that is optimized for the kinds of thing we want to do in data analysis. That is, we want to efficiently query a big dataset lots of different ways, rather than, say, repeatedly update its records as fast as possible. We can work in R and write tidy dplyr-like queries that get handled by the database. It’s great.

We can ask all kinds of questions of data like this. We also have to be careful with it, just because any dataset that’s this large and has grown over this long a period will have all kinds of quirks in it. For example, the classification scheme the city uses to categorize service requests isn’t static, and for some categories it gets completely redone. At least once over the period the city changed the service provider for data management, which affected measurement in some ways. Meanwhile, on the complaints side, one feature of service databases like this is that some people really like to complain, even by the high standards of New Yorkers. Complaining also becomes easier after the introduction of the web portal, because you can just quickly report something via a form rather than having to make a phone call. So we need to think about how to deal with things like that.

Complaints are ultimately made by individual people, and our dataset is a record of individual reports. But here I’m going to aggregate things to the level of neighborhoods. You can slice up the city in many different ways. New York often uses Neighborhood Tabulation Areas, or NTAs, as its de facto neighborhood unit. The idea is to get something that’s larger than a Census Tract, of which there are about 2,300 in New York, but smaller than one of the City’s 59 Community Districts. There are 262 NTAs, of which 197 are residential. Here’s a map of them, with their names.

So, how can we get from our complaint records to an NTA-level map, and what do we want to see? As I say, here we’re going more or less for data-driven neighborhood trolling, so here’s what I did to characterize each neighborhood. First, I did a fair amount of work harmonizing the complaint categories over the whole dataset, but in addition to that here I’ll just restrict myself to complaints from 2022 to 2025, which is about 13.5m records. Second, we want to moderate the role played by people we can politely call “super-reporters”, so we count distinct addresses within complaint categories, within residential NTAs, over the time period we’re looking at. Each address counts only once in each category it complained about, so we get about 4.6m address-category pairs from about one million unique addresses. (The addresses don’t include identifying information like house or apartment numbers, by the way.) The average address complains in about four or five categories over the four years we’re looking at.

Now, when it comes to complaints, we are all trying to get through this thing we call life and many of the trials we face, we all share. Which is to say that the most common complaints in any given neighborhood are more likely to be the most common complaints in other neighborhoods, too. These are things like the heat and hot water being out, noise of various kinds, and illegal parking. But what we’re interested in is the most distinctive complaints in each neighborhood. So we take every complaint and figure out its share of all complaints citywide. Then we do the same but within each neighborhood. And then for each neighborhood we ask, what category of complaint in this neighborhood most exceeds its citywide share? Actually we do two things. We do that first by general category of complaint, like “Sanitation and Dumping”, or “Parking, Driveways, and Vehicles”, or “Buildings and Construction”. And then we do it for the most fine-grained category we have, like “Traffic: Drag Racing”, or “Appliance: Refrigerator”, or “Lost Property in Taxi or For-Hire Vehicle: Wallet”. Then we color our NTA map in by the broad category and label each neighborhood by its most-specific category. Here’s what that looks like.

I think the results are pretty good. Sorry about the small print and fine detail. This is the sort of thing that works best as a poster. But zoom in and take a look. And of course Tag Yourself. Are you the Badly Behaved Nightlife Crescent from the Upper East Side to Lower Manhattan who got drunk and lost your wallet or keys? (I like how right at the top of the UES they don’t lose their wallets but they do complain about the driver.) Are you the brownstone Brooklyn Bicycle Police? Or the South Brooklyn Curb Cutters who are installing illegal carports? Or maybe you are just out in Woodside, Elmhurst, or Corona, drinking in public. Or abandoning a vehicle somewhere. There’s a lot going on in the city.

Bear in mind that there’s a kind of duality to the map, in the sense that at first glance it shows you what seems to be happening in these NTAs, but only through the lens of what people complain about in these neighborhoods. So, indulge your neighborhood stereotypes, but maybe don’t lean to hard on them. Though I do like those people in Forest Hills who just like to call the cops for unspecified Other Non-Emergency Police Matters. Like, for a chat or something. What else are you gonna do out there on a Friday?

items.title: When Do Causal ML Models Beat LM / GLM / GBM?
items.author: Philipp Probst
items.description:
Summary



Continue reading: When Do Causal ML Models Beat LM / GLM / GBM?
items.content:
[This article was first published on blog_philipppro, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Summary

Who this is for: Data scientists and analysts who need to estimate what an intervention does (a call, a discount, a campaign) and want to know when causal ML methods are worth using over LM, GLM, and GBM. The basis is nine simulations with a known true effect, each with 40 repetitions.

The five most important findings

  1. Data first, algorithm second. If the model contains a wrong variable or omits an important influencing factor, all methods are equally wrong, including the most flexible ones. Only domain knowledge or an instrument helps here (Cases 4, 5).
  2. For the average effect, causal ML wins only when influencing factors act nonlinearly. In that case the LM is clearly biased and Double ML is almost right. The difference comes from the construction principle (first adjust, then estimate), not from a particular algorithm (Case 3).
  3. A risk model is not an effect model. Calling the customers with the highest cancellation risk achieves less than a random selection, because precisely these customers are hardly retainable any more (Case 7).
  4. The correct ranking is easier than the correct magnitude. A simple GLM can select the right units and still misstate the size of the effect (Case 9).
  5. The causal forest pays off when the size of the effect per unit matters and its form is unknown (Cases 8, 9). In simple worlds, a well-specified GLM is better (Case 6).

How to read this report?

  • Choose a method: Guide (next section), with two decision trees and a table.
  • Understand the methods: Methodology, with terms, formulas, strengths and weaknesses, and the question of how to check without a known effect.
  • Verify the evidence: Simulation, with nine cases, each with data, results, and a lesson.
  • The numbers [n] in the text refer to the references at the end.

Guide: Which Method When?

Work through the steps from top to bottom. Stop at the first point where the answer is “not possible”: no algorithm decides steps 1–3; only step 4 chooses the method. “Unit” stands for anything that is treated (customer, person, contract, branch); the examples in the cases are set at a fictional online fitness subscription service (an app with training plans and classes).

The terms used in the guide:

  • A/B test: Who is treated was determined at random (technical term: randomized). Treated and untreated units are therefore comparable.
  • No random assignment (called “non-random” for short in the table): The treatment followed rules or judgments; the data simply accumulated (technical term: observational data). Treated and untreated units already differ beforehand.
  • Influencing variable (confounder): A variable that influences who is treated and the outcome. Measured means it is in the data. Not measured: It is missing, and no algorithm can replace it.
  • Instrument: A random nudge that shifts the treatment but affects the outcome only through it (e.g. a randomly sent invitation). Allows an estimate even though a confounder is missing.
  • Average: A single effect for all units together (technical term: ATE). Answer to “Does the intervention work on average?”.
  • Ranking (targeting): Deciding whom to treat, e.g. the 30% with the largest effect. Only who comes first matters; a model may over- or underestimate the effect by the same amount for everyone.
  • Effect per unit (CATE): The exact size of the effect for each unit, e.g. to weigh costs and benefits per unit. Stricter than the ranking: A model can rank correctly and still estimate the size wrongly (Case 9).

Blue = question, green = recommendation, red = stop.

Step 1 – What is the decision?

Question Target quantity Next
Does the intervention work on average? Average (ATE) Step 2
Whom should I treat? Ranking of units by effect Step 2
How large is the effect for this unit? (e.g. for cost-benefit per unit) Effect per unit (CATE) Step 2
Who will cancel? (without intervention) Risk, no effect Pure GBM, done. Unsuitable for decisions about interventions (Case 7: top-30% uplift 0.037, worse than chance).
How strongly should I treat? (e.g. discount level) Dose-response curve Methodological knowledge, not simulated (see conclusion, continuous treatment).

Step 2 – How was the treatment assigned?

  • At random (A/B test, lottery): Identification is secured, continue with step 4.
  • By rules or by judgment of the business department (no random assignment): continue with step 3.
  • Randomly assigned, but not everyone received the treatment (e.g. call assigned, customer not reached): The comparison of means by assignment measures the effect of the assignment. For the effect of the treatment itself, the assignment serves as an instrument (2SLS, Case 5 [5]). Not simulated.

Step 3 – Identification (only without random assignment)

This is where most projects fail, and no algorithm helps.

Three terms decide which variables belong in the model. They differ only in where the variable sits in the cause-and-effect picture ( = treatment, = outcome, = the variable in question):

Term Structure What is it? Example In the model?
Confounder \(T \leftarrow X \rightarrow Y\) A common cause: \(X\) influences who is treated and the outcome. Treated and untreated units therefore already differ before the treatment. Age: Older customers are more likely to receive a call and, for their own reasons, cancel more or less often. Yes. Otherwise the influence of \(X\) is read as an effect of \(T\) (bias). For nonlinear influence, also in the right form (Case 2, 3).
Mediator \(T \rightarrow X \rightarrow Y\) An intermediate station: \(T\) acts on \(Y\) through \(X\). \(X\) only arises after the treatment and carries part of the effect. Call \(\rightarrow\) customer sets up a training plan \(\rightarrow\) stays. “Training plan set up” is the mediator. No, if the total effect is of interest. Otherwise the part that runs through \(X\) is missing (Case 4).
Collider \(T \rightarrow X \leftarrow Y\) A common consequence: \(X\) is influenced by \(T\) and by \(Y\). \(X\) arises after both. Call and cancellation both lead to the customer ending up in the complaint log. “In the complaint log” is the collider. No. Otherwise a spurious relationship between \(T\) and \(Y\) arises. Not simulated as a separate case; same rule as for the mediator.

Rule of thumb: What exists before the treatment and co-determines it belongs in the model. What arises after the treatment does not. Whether a variable is a confounder or a mediator is not revealed by the data – it is domain knowledge about the process.

  1. Which variables go into the model? What exists before the treatment and co-determines it goes in (confounder). What arises after the treatment stays out (mediator, collider). The data do not say which is which; this is domain knowledge. In Case 4 all algorithms are equally biased when the mediator is included. Overview of good and bad control variables: [19]. Tool: Draw the process as a DAG in DAGitty; the program names the required variables [26].
  2. Is a confounder missing? Cannot be proven from the data. Hints come from the placebo test (an outcome that the treatment cannot influence must show effect 0; Case 5) and the E-value (how strong a missing confounder would have to be to explain away the effect) [20]. DoWhy runs such tests automatically [27].
  3. If one is missing, is there an instrument? A random nudge that acts only through the treatment. Yes: 2SLS for a constant effect, Instrumental forest for a varying effect (Case 5). Validity cannot be checked from the data. No: no causal statement. Label the number as an association, not as an effect. Exception: If before-after data or a threshold exist, see difference-in-differences and regression discontinuity under “Further methods (not simulated)”.
  4. Overlap: Are there treated and untreated units in every group? Check with the propensity histogram (section “Overlap diagnostic”). Propensities near 0 or 1: restrict the population to the region with overlap. AIPW and other weighting estimators otherwise become unstable (Case 3, †). The restriction itself is not simulated here.

Step 4 – Choose a method

First find the data situation (column 2) and the question (column 3); the terms are defined at the beginning of the guide.

As a decision tree, from top to bottom (blue = question, green = recommendation, red = stop; Var. = variables). It presupposes that step 3 is passed (including overlap) and that the question concerns an effect, not pure risk. With little data (a few hundred units), row 2 of the table applies. The table additionally lists a cross-check and what to avoid:

# Data situation Question Recommendation Cross-check Avoid Evidence
1 A/B test Average Comparison of means. LM (T + X) at most for variance reduction. – – Case 1, 6–8
2 A/B test, little data (a few hundred) Ranking or effect per unit First check whether the effect varies at all. Without a strong prior hypothesis, use the average for everyone (LM T + X, CATE-RMSE 0.141 in Case 1). Causal forest (0.21): estimates an almost constant effect when the effect is constant T-learner and GBM S-learner (CATE-RMSE 0.72 and 0.51, respectively): invent differences from noise Case 1
3 A/B test, few variables, simple form plausible Ranking or effect per unit GLM with T x X (CATE-RMSE 0.127 vs. causal forest 0.24). S-learner, causal forest Pure risk model (Case 7) Case 6, 7
4 A/B test, many variables, form unknown Ranking S-learner (top-30% uplift 1.64 vs. oracle 1.65). Causal forest, R-learner (equally good selection) Double ML and AIPW (only deliver an average), pure risk model Case 8
5 A/B test, many variables, form unknown Effect per unit Causal forest (CATE-RMSE 0.28 vs. S-learner 0.45). Also provides confidence intervals. R-learner (0.36) GLM with T x X (0.74) or with all 2-way interactions (1.08) Case 8
6 No randomization; confounders measured, linear Average LM (T + X). Double ML Naive comparison Case 2
7 No randomization; confounders measured, nonlinear or unknown Average Double ML with a GBM as building block. AIPW, causal forest LM and S-learner (biased) Case 3
8 No randomization; confounders measured Ranking R- or S-learner (top-30% uplift 2.70 and 2.71, respectively, vs. oracle 2.74). Causal forest Pure risk model Case 9
9 No randomization; confounders measured Effect per unit Causal forest (ATE bias -0.020, CATE-RMSE 0.26). R-learner (0.34) LM/GLM (ATE bias -1.76: ranks correctly, size wrong). AIPW: no result in 21 of 40 runs. Case 9
10 No randomization; confounder missing, instrument available Average 2SLS (constant effect) or Instrumental forest (varying effect). Placebo test (Case 5) All methods without an instrument Case 5
11 No randomization; confounder missing, no instrument Any question about the effect No causal method. Report the association, E-value as sensitivity analysis. Exception: With before-after data or a threshold, difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity are possible (not simulated). – Any method that outputs an effect number Case 5

Step 5 – Check without knowing the truth

  • A/B test: Qini/uplift curve and calibration on a hold-out dataset are valid.
  • No random assignment: R-loss ranks the methods only as long as step 3 holds. In addition, placebo test and overlap histogram.
  • Agreement of several methods proves nothing: In Cases 4 and 5 all methods agree and are wrong.
  • State the uncertainty: An estimate should come with a confidence interval (Methodology, “Confidence intervals”). It measures only the random error: If step 3 is violated, even a narrow interval misses the target.

Details in the section “Evaluation without knowing the truth”.

Step 6 – When in doubt

Keep the simplest correct model as the baseline. Adopt the more complex method only if it is clearly better on validated data. In Cases 1, 2 and 6, complexity brings nothing.

Not tested (statements about these are methodological knowledge, not simulation): more than 100 variables with weak heterogeneity, trimming under weak overlap, weak instrument, incomplete compliance, panel/time structures, multiple treatment levels, continuous treatment, and the methods in the section “Further methods (not simulated)” (e.g. BART, BCF, TMLE).

Other decision aids

A fully automatic decision tree that chooses the right method from the data alone does not exist, and cannot exist: Whether a variable is a confounder or a mediator is not in the data (Case 4). Any automation therefore needs a cause-and-effect picture (DAG) based on domain knowledge as input. What does exist:

  • DAGitty [26]: You draw the DAG; the program names the variables that must go into the model, and possible instruments. Automates step 3.1.
  • DoWhy [27]: From the DAG through identification and estimation to automatic checks (placebo, random additional confounder, subsamples). Closest to an automatic workflow.
  • EconML Library Flow Chart [28]: Decision tree for choosing the estimator, similar to the one in step 4. Additionally asks about compliance and whether the effect depends linearly on the features.
  • Causal Roadmap [24] and Target Trial Emulation [25]: standardized workflows from epidemiology. You first describe the experiment you would have liked to run, and then check how close the data come to it.
  • Automatic model selection for CATE (e.g. causaltune based on EconML): chooses the estimator via R-loss or similar measures. This works only if identification holds (see “Evaluation without knowing the truth”).

Methodology

This part describes what is estimated and with which methods, without simulation results: the core idea, the terms, the methods studied with their formulas, and the question of how to check a method on real data (where the true effect is unknown).

Core idea

LM, GLM, and GBM are normally trained to predict Y. CausalML models are built to estimate the effect of a treatment T on Y, either on average (ATE) or per unit (CATE). A good prediction model is not automatically a good effect model. Conversely, an effect model is not automatically better when the world is simple.

In real data the true effect is never known. That is why we simulate here: we define the formulas that generate the data ourselves. We therefore know the true effect of every single unit and can measure each method against it exactly.

Classification following Molnar [6]: the report takes the causal inference mindset (what causes what?) and uses supervised learning (prediction models such as GBM) only as a building block, e.g. in Double ML. Evaluation is frequentist (bias and spread over repeated samples). Other mindsets lead to other tools: Bayesian to BART and Bayesian causal forest (uncertainty per unit as a posterior), reinforcement learning to bandits, which assign the treatment continuously and learn while doing so. That is a different type of data than the one used here. The core message in this language: a good supervised-learning model is not automatically a good causal-inference model. Introductions to the field: [1, 2, 3].

Terms

Potential outcomes. Every unit has two possible outcomes: if it is treated () and if not (). Only one of them is ever observed. The individual effect is .

Term Definition
ATE (Average Treatment Effect) \(\text{ATE} = E[Y(1) – Y(0)]\): effect on average across all units.
CATE (Conditional ATE) \(\tau(x) = E[Y(1) – Y(0) \mid X = x]\): effect for units with characteristics \(x\). This is the effect “per unit”.
Treatment \(T\) The action whose effect we are interested in (call, discount, campaign). Always 0/1 here.
Outcome \(Y\) The outcome the action is supposed to influence. Higher = better.
Confounder Variable that influences both T and Y (\(T \leftarrow X \rightarrow Y\)). If it is ignored, the comparison of treated vs. untreated mixes the effect of T with the effect of X. Must be in the model, and in the correct functional form.
Mediator Variable on the path from T to Y (\(T \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\)); it arises after T. Adjusting for it removes the part of the effect that runs through M. Must not be in the model if the total effect is of interest.
Collider Variable that is influenced by T and Y (\(T \rightarrow C \leftarrow Y\)). Adjusting for it creates a spurious relationship between T and Y. Must not be in the model. (Not a separate case here; same rule as for the mediator: nothing that arises after T.)
Instrument \(Z\) Variable that influences T but affects Y only through T (\(Z \rightarrow T \rightarrow Y\)) and is unrelated to unobserved disturbances. Allows effect estimation despite unobserved confounding.
Effect modifier Variable on which the size of the effect depends (e.g. the discount only works for price-sensitive customers). Creates heterogeneity: \(\tau(x)\) is not constant.
Noise variable Variable with no influence on T or Y. Does not harm systematically, but costs estimation precision.
Randomization T is assigned by chance (coin flip). Then there are no confounders for T, and the simple comparison of means is unbiased.

In the diagrams (DAGs) below, an arrow means: “A enters the formula of B”. Dashed = unobserved variable.

Methods

All methods receive the training data as input and return an estimated effect for every test customer as output. Exception: the “pure” GBM, which ignores T and only predicts a risk.

Method Model Assumption
Naive (diff. in means) \(\hat\tau = \bar Y_{T=1} – \bar Y_{T=0}\) No confounding (randomization)
LM/GLM (T + X) \(Y = \beta_0 + \tau T + \beta^\top X\) Effect constant; Y linear in X (logit-linear for binary Y)
LM/GLM (T x X) \(Y = \beta_0 + \tau_0 T + \beta^\top X + T \cdot \gamma^\top X\) Effect linear in X
LM/GLM (T x all 2-way X) like T x X, plus all products \(X_j X_k\) and their interaction with T Effect quadratic in X
GBM / LightGBM S-learner \(\hat f(X, T)\) = one GBM with T as a feature; \(\hat\tau(x) = \hat f(x, 1) – \hat f(x, 0)\) No form imposed. Regularization can push the effect of T toward 0.
GBM / LightGBM T-learner \(\hat f_1\) on treated, \(\hat f_0\) on untreated; \(\hat\tau(x) = \hat f_1(x) – \hat f_0(x)\) No form imposed. Two separate models, each with half the data: high variance.
GBM / LightGBM pure (ignores T) \(\hat f(X)\) without T; score = predicted risk \(-\hat f(x)\) No effect model. This is how targeting is often done (churn model, then call the highest-risk units).
Causal forest grf::causal_forest No form imposed. Estimates \(\tau(x)\) directly, adjusted for propensity and baseline (honest trees). Default settings. ATE here = mean of the CATE predictions.
Double ML (xgboost) Cross-fitting (5 folds): \(\hat\ell(X) \approx E[Y \mid X]\), \(\hat m(X) \approx E[T \mid X]\) via xgboost; \(\hat\tau = \frac{\sum_i (T_i – \hat m_i)(Y_i – \hat\ell_i)}{\sum_i (T_i – \hat m_i)^2}\) Effect constant (or weighted mean); confounders arbitrarily nonlinear. Same xgboost as the S-learner, but T and Y are first residualized on X, so regularization does not bias the effect.

Methods in detail

The methods from the S-learner onward, each with the idea, the formula, and the typical weakness. Common notation: is the expected outcome, the propensity (probability of being treated), and denotes estimated.

GBM S-learner (“Single”)

A single model for all units, with as one feature among many. The effect is the difference in the prediction when is set from 0 to 1 and everything else is held fixed.

Weakness: If has only a small influence, the GBM barely uses it (regularization), and the effect is pushed toward 0. Under strong confounding a residual bias remains (Case 3). Source: [9].

GBM T-learner (“Two”)

Two separate models: one only on the treated, one only on the untreated. The effect is the difference between the two predictions.

Weakness: Each model sees only part of the data, and the two errors add up. With small n or groups of unequal size this is very noisy (Case 1). The X-learner (see “Further methods”) addresses exactly this. Source: [9].

Pure GBM (ignores )

An ordinary prediction model for without , e.g. a churn model. The score is the predicted risk.

Weakness: It answers “who is at risk?”, not “for whom does the treatment work?”. Units with high risk may be unpersuadable (Case 7). On the difference between risk and uplift models: [21].

Double ML

Two nuisance models predict from what is to be expected without the treatment: the outcome and the assignment . What remains is only what does not explain (the residuals). The effect is the slope between the two residuals.

Cross-fitting: The nuisance models predict each unit using models that have not seen it (5 folds). Otherwise overfitting would distort the residuals. Why it works: Errors in and enter only as a product, so the form of the confounders can be learned freely without biasing the effect. Weakness: a single effect for everyone (the average), no effect per unit. Source: [7]; textbook: [2].

R-learner (Double ML with per-unit effect)

The same residuals as in Double ML, but the effect is no longer a single number but a function learned by an arbitrary model. It is chosen so that the residuals of are explained as well as possible by :

Implemented as a weighted regression: an xgboost predicts from , with weight . Weakness: Units with (propensity near 0 or 1) contribute almost nothing; with a constant effect the model learns heterogeneity that does not exist (more variance than Double ML). Source: [8].

Causal forest

A forest of trees that are split so that the effect differs as much as possible between the leaves (not the outcome). For a new unit , the forest counts which training units often lands in the same leaf with (weight ) and estimates the effect only from these similar units, again using the residuals as in Double ML:

Honest: One half of the data determines the splits, the other half estimates the effect. This prevents the forest from learning random fluctuations as an effect. Weakness: needs a lot of data to find fine differences; with a constant effect or a linear world there is no advantage. Sources: [10, 11]; honest trees: [12].

AIPW (doubly robust)

Combines two models. The outcome model predicts both outcomes for every unit. The weighted correction offsets deviations at the units actually observed, with rare cases (small propensity) counting more.

Doubly robust: The result is correct if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correct. Weakness: If is near 0 or 1, the weights explode (Case 3, individual runs fail). Average effect only. Source: [13]; TMLE as a more stable variant: [17].

2SLS (instrument )

If a confounder is unobserved, an instrument helps: it shifts but has no other path to . Stage 1 isolates the part of that explains. Stage 2 uses only this part, which is free of the unobserved confounder.

Without and with a binary , this is the Wald estimator: the effect of on , divided by the effect of on .

Weakness: Whether is valid cannot be tested from the data. If is weak (barely shifts ), the denominator is near 0 and the estimate is very uncertain. Source: [5].

Instrumental forest

The same principle as 2SLS, but local as in the causal forest: for each unit , a separate IV estimator is computed from the similar units (weights of the forest). The effect may therefore depend on .

Weakness: With a constant effect it is merely noisier than 2SLS (Case 5). Source: [11].

Evaluation methods

In real data the true effect is unknown. What can be checked depends on whether the treatment was assigned at random.

With randomized data (e.g., a randomly treated share of a campaign), the difference in means is unbiased and serves as the benchmark. On a hold-out set, any effect model can then be checked from the outside:

  • Calibration: Group units into deciles by predicted effect and compute the actual difference in means within each decile. If prediction and measurement agree, the model is usable (grf: test_calibration).
  • Uplift or Qini curve: Do the top X % according to the model really have the higher effect? This is the practical version of the top-30% measure in this report [21].
  • Comparison with chance: The benefit of selecting by model is compared with random selection and with “treat everyone”.

A permanently small random share (e.g., 5–10 %) costs something, but it is the only clean answer.

With observational data there is no such benchmark. The following tools narrow down errors but prove nothing, and none of them is recommended across the board: each works only under its own assumptions or is too noisy to decide on its own. It is best to combine several.

  • Test on your own data (“plasmode”): keep the real features and the real assignment , regenerate with an effect of your own choosing, and measure the methods against it. This is what this report does on a small scale, only with the structure of your own data. The result holds only for the chosen effect form, however.

  • Loss function on hold-out data: The R-loss [8, 22] (or the analogous DR-loss [14]) compares effect models without knowing the true effect. It is noisy and depends on the nuisance models : usable for discarding poor models, but for picking the best one only when the differences are clear (see Simulation: “Evaluation without knowing the truth”).

    Step 1: nuisance models. Two prediction models are learned on the training data, the outcome model and the treatment model (propensity).

    Step 2: residuals on the hold-out set. From and , subtract what can already be predicted from :

    What remains is only the part of not explained by and the part of that is “random”. If the treatment acts with , then approximately .

    Step 3: loss. An effect model is then judged by how well it fits this relationship:

    Smaller is better. For comparison, (no effect) gives . A method is useful only if it falls below this value. The loss needs neither the true effect nor randomization, but it presupposes that contains all confounders (otherwise Cases 4 and 5).

  • Agreement of several methods: Similar results from LM, Double ML and causal forest are reassuring; clear deviations point to a wrong functional form or weak overlap. It is not proof (Cases 4, 5: all equally wrong).

  • Overlap and balance: Histogram of the estimated propensity (values near 0 or 1 are a warning sign, Case 3) and comparison of the features of treated and untreated units after weighting. This checks only measured variables.

  • Placebo test: The treatment is applied to an outcome it cannot affect (or to a period before it). An “effect” indicates remaining confounding. It requires a credible placebo outcome, which is rarely available.

  • Sensitivity analysis (e.g., E-value, Rosenbaum): How strong would an unobserved confounder have to be to explain the effect away? This yields an order of magnitude, not a decision [20].

  • Comparison with an experiment: If a small randomized test exists somewhere, the observational estimator is measured against it. This holds only if population and treatment are similar enough.

Not testable is whether all confounders are measured and no mediators are in the model. No quality measure detects this; predictive accuracy can even look good (see “Predictive accuracy is not effect accuracy”). This is decided by domain knowledge of the process, not by the method.

Confidence intervals

A confidence interval shows how much an estimate would vary from sample to sample. A 95 % interval is usually the estimate ± 1.96 standard errors (SE). It measures only random error, not systematic error: if a wrong variable is in the model or a driver is missing, a narrow interval will surely surround the wrong value (see Simulation, “Do the confidence intervals hold?”).

Here the methods are measured on nine simulated worlds in which the true effect is known. First the setup, then the cases in four blocks, then the overall comparison and the conclusion.

Setup

How are methods scored?

For each case, a training dataset with new random numbers is generated 40 times. Each method is trained on it and compared with the known true effect on a separate test dataset (n = 5000).

What matters is thus not the learning algorithm but the construction of the estimator. If you know the form, the LM with the right term wins again.

Case 5 – Unobserved confounding

Story. Customers can voluntarily take part in an 8-week training program (T). More motivated customers (U) are more likely to take part and also train more without the program (Y = activity score). U is not recorded anywhere. As part of an experiment, however, an invitation Z was sent at random, which strongly increases participation. Z is an instrument.

Data generation (n = 2000, observational data with randomized invitation):

Model input: for all standard methods; for 2SLS and the instrumental forest. U is never in the input.

True effect: for everyone, ATE = 1.

Why all standard methods fail: Participants are more motivated (higher U). Without U, no model can separate which part of the difference comes from the program and which from U. Why the instrument helps: Z is assigned at random, hence independent of U. It changes the participation rate from 0.26 to 0.74 and acts on Y only through T. The three conditions: Z affects T (testable), Z is random (here by design), Z acts only through T (not testable, an assumption).

Correct estimation: 2SLS with instrument Z (T ~ Z + X1, then Y ~ T_hat + X1). The instrumental forest is only needed if the effect additionally depends on X.

If a point lies on the dashed line, the prediction agrees with the experiment. The calibration slope (red line) summarizes this: 1 = calibrated, > 1 = predictions compressed too much, < 1 = spread too much. Calibration thus shows not only whether the effect is right but also in which direction a model is off. Constant estimators (Double ML, AIPW) have no spread and cannot be checked this way.

Where identification fails, not a single interval contains the true effect: the difference in means without random assignment (Cases 2, 3, 9), the LM with nonlinear predictors (Cases 3, 9), all adjusted methods with a mediator (Case 4), and all methods without an instrument when a variable is missing (Case 5). In Case 4, it is the simple difference in means that is correct, precisely because it does not use the mediator. A narrow interval is therefore no sign that the estimate is right.

Conclusion

When does CausalML pay off?

CausalML methods pay off when predictors act nonlinearly (Cases 3, 9), when the effect depends on many variables in an unknown form and its magnitude per unit matters (Cases 8, 9), and, for selection, only when the model includes the treatment (Case 7). They bring no advantage with small samples and in linear worlds (Cases 1, 2, 6), with a wrong choice of variables (Case 4), and with a missing variable without an instrument (Case 5). How to choose a method from this is explained in the guide; what has not been tested is listed in the box at the end of the guide.

Continuous treatment

Example: discount size instead of discount yes/no. In all cases, is binary; what follows is methodological knowledge, not a simulation. The rules on confounder, mediator and collider apply unchanged. The question changes: the target is a dose-response curve or the slope , and “whom to treat?” becomes “how much?”. LM/GLM, S-learner, Double ML (residuals instead of the propensity), causal forest and 2SLS can be carried over to continuous ; the T-learner and the difference in means cannot, and AIPW only via a generalized propensity density (unstable with thin overlap). Double ML and causal forest assume the effect to be linear in . If the effect saturates, they return a mean slope that is correct at no dose; the model must then learn the shape of the curve (S-learner, splines). Overlap here means: every relevant dose must occur among comparable customers; outside the observed range, every estimate is extrapolation.

Limitations

  • The results apply to these data-generating processes. The ranking of the methods depends on the setup, not on a fixed hierarchy.
  • The ATE of the row “Causal forest” is the mean of its CATE predictions on the test data set; the doubly robust estimator is listed separately as “AIPW (causal forest)”. Double ML (without an effect model) and AIPW deliver only an average effect; their CATE-RMSE is therefore poor by construction when the effect is heterogeneous, and their top-30% uplift corresponds to a random selection.
  • In Case 3, overlap is weak at the extremes (for , the propensity is close to 1). This makes the case harder for all methods, not easier.
  • In real data, the true effect is never known; only proxy validation is possible there (e.g., uplift curves on randomized data).
  • A much larger study of the same kind, with dozens of methods and teams, is the ACIC competition [23]. It reaches the same basic finding: flexible methods help with estimation, but no method wins everywhere.
